rv.q: The show is inoffensive, insubstantial, very sporadically amusing and breezily directed by Mark Gatiss, who happens to be Hallard’s husband.
This is superficial froth – not something, in my view, you could ever say about Abba.
This play is an absolute delight; it is a very well written and hilarious ode to ABBA.
Hallard manages to pull the play back near the end by reminding us of the fun of these super troupers.
The problem with The Way Old Friends Do is that the comedy often isn’t very funny.
The Way Old Friends Do trades on an audience’s natural kinship with its subject and then, much like Christian in the play, betrays that trust.
The whole thing is lacking in inspiration and heart; it’s not funny enough to be a jolly romp, and ABBA fans would be better off at Mamma Mia! or ABBA Voyage.
Few shows get it right as effortlessly as The Way Old Friends Do.
The Way Old Friends Do is a gorgeously realised super trouper of a play that’s well worth taking a chance on.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this ABBA-themed comedy about a drag tribute band, with some charmed by its camp celebration of friendship while others find it fatuous and threadbare, questioning whether London needs yet another show built around the Swedish supergroup.
